title: Delhi Police facial recognition trial matches 2,930 missing children in four days, but no case is cracked
summary: MWCD affidavit: FRS run on 45,000 children in homes matched 2,930 identities on 6–10 April 2018; on 22 January 2019 the Delhi High Court recorded that the software had not cracked any case.
account: PTI reported on 22 April 2018 (Business Standard) that the Ministry of Women and Child Development told the Delhi High Court in an affidavit that the Delhi Police, “on a trial basis, used the FRS on 45,000 children living in different children's homes”, and that 2,930 children “could be recognized between April 6 and April 10”; the ministry's secretary Rakesh Srivastava said the police shared the outcome on 10 April, which is the date used here. The ministry had supplied data on about seven lakh missing children from the Track Child portal after the court, in Sadhan Haldar v NCT of Delhi, pressed the police to test-run facial recognition. The same report says identities “have been established and efforts are on to help them reunite with their families”; no reunification is documented in any source on file. The Wire (republished by the Pulitzer Center, 2–3 July 2025), citing the Bureau of Police Research and Development's Compendium of Equipment, says the police bought two facial recognition systems on 28 March 2018, manufactured by Innefu Labs and supplied by Pelorus Technologies, and quotes an Innefu blog claiming its AI Vision product “helped in identifying 3000 missing children” in its first four days. On 23 August 2018 Delhi Police counsel Rahul Mehra told the High Court, in a habeas corpus matter about women missing from a placement agency, “The software is not good. There is only two percent match” (NDTV). On 22 January 2019 the High Court (Hima Kohli and Manoj Kumar Ohri JJ) recorded in Sadhan Haldar that it was told the software “has not helped in cracking any case of missing children so far”, against 5,160 children untraced out of 19,916 reported missing in 2016–2018. The earlier reviewer's reason cites a Centre for Internet and Society (CIS India) report giving 10,617 matches of which 3,202 identities were verified and no reunification count; that PDF was not located in this pass. Existing record AIBD-0126 concerns a different Delhi Police facial recognition case.
purpose: Procured under the Delhi High Court's direction in Sadhan Haldar to match photographs of missing and found children against the Track Child database; the April 2018 trial run was that intended use.
system: Delhi Police Facial Recognition System (reported by The Wire as Innefu Labs' AI Vision)
developer: Innefu Labs Pvt Ltd (manufacturer, per The Wire citing the BPR&D Compendium of Equipment); supplied by Pelorus Technologies Pvt Ltd
deployer: Delhi Police (Crime Branch), using Ministry of Women and Child Development Track Child portal data
domain: Policing / missing persons and child protection
taxonomy_note: Loose fit; the only documented outcome is a raw match count that the police and the High Court later undercut.

ratings.reason: No source on file documents a child reunited with a family as a result of the 2,930 matches; the High Court recorded on 22 January 2019 that the software had not cracked any missing-child case.
The police reported 2,930 identities “established” to the ministry; the same police told the court four months later that the software produced only a two percent match.
The court's own figures (5,160 children untraced of 19,916 reported in 2016–2018) are the context; no reduction attributable to the software is documented.

ai_role.statement: The software produced the 2,930 matches reported in the ministry's affidavit; the claim rests on the police's report of raw output, relayed by PTI, and on the vendor's blog. No source on file verifies a single match to a reunification, the police counsel described the match rate as two percent in August 2018, and the Delhi High Court recorded in January 2019 that the software had not helped crack any case. The earlier reviewer's CIS India figures (10,617 matches, 3,202 identities verified) were not re-read.

later.quote: “We are told that the use of ‘Facial Recognition Software’ has not helped in cracking any case of missing children so far, which comes as a surprise. It is most unacceptable that the software adopted by the Delhi Police after due diligence has not borne any results.”
